name: Perma
purpose: Link-preservation service and platform: captures a cited web page and issues a permanent 'perma link' that resolves to the archived copy, designed for legal and scholarly citation.
journalism_use_case: Preserve cited sources as stable links so a published investigation does not rot when the source page changes or disappears — the reader clicking a citation three years later sees what you saw, which is a basic integrity property most published journalism lacks.
pros: Solves link rot in published work, which is a real and under-addressed problem: a story whose sources have all 404'd is much harder to defend
Institutional durability: Harvard LIL and a library consortium behind it, which is a better continuity bet than a startup or a volunteer project
Perma links are recognised in legal and scholarly citation practice, so they carry conventional authority
Open source (MIT AND GPL-3.0 dual, per README) and self-hostable in principle
cons: Self-hosting is heavy — a Django stack plus storage — and the hosted service is the realistic path for almost everyone
On perma.cc, captures and target URLs are held by Harvard LIL and the links are public, so using it discloses what you cited and when; for a pre-publication investigation that is a leak
Licence is declared in the README rather than a LICENSE file (GitHub reports no SPDX), so the dual MIT/GPL-3.0 position needs confirmation for compliance records
Hosted access requires a perma.cc account with institutional tiers whose current prices were not verified in this survey; 95 open issues and no release objects (latest tag v-.59.1)
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 540 stars with 95 open issues, no release objects, SPDX none with licensing declared in the README, last push 2026-11-16. Perma.cc's adoption in legal citation is well established in that field, which is relevant institutional evidence.
assessment: Use the hosted service at publication time, not during reporting — that distinction is the whole operational guidance. A perma link created while you are still investigating publicly records your interest in a URL; created at publication, it is exactly the right artefact. For your profile I would pair it with your own Scoop or ArchiveBox capture so you are not solely dependent on a third party for your evidence of record, and confirm the licence position in writing if you ever plan to self-host.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, no release objects, latest tag v-.59.1, SPDX none, 540 stars, 95 open issues. Current commits with an operating hosted service and institutional backing; release engineering is informal because the service, not the package, is the product.
licence: MIT AND GPL-3.0 (dual, per README; GitHub reports no SPDX and there is no LICENSE file)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Archived content belongs to the original publishers.
licence_restrictions: Dual-licence position is declared only in the README, which is weak for compliance purposes — confirm with the maintainers before self-hosting or redistributing. The GPL-3.0 element would constrain a proprietary derivative.
costs: Hosted perma.cc uses institutional tiers (library and organisation subscriptions) whose current prices were NOT verified in this survey — check before budgeting. Self-hosting: no software fee but a Django stack plus storage, realistically a multi-VM deployment. Assumptions for self-hosting: moderate capture volume.
privacy: On perma.cc, captures and target URLs are held by Harvard LIL and the resulting links are public — so creating a perma link publishes the fact that someone archived that URL at that time. Appropriate at publication, inappropriate during a confidential investigation.
alternatives: Scoop (same lab) for provenance-attested local captures with no disclosure
ArchiveBox for a self-hosted archive of everything you cite
Internet Archive 'Save Page Now' as a free public alternative, with the same disclosure caveat
blockers: Hosted captures and links are public — discloses what you archived and when
summary: Link-preservation service and platform: captures a cited web page and issues a permanent 'perma link'…

name: SingleFile
purpose: Browser extension (and CLI) that saves a complete web page as a single self-contained HTML file with all assets inlined, preserving the page exactly as rendered.
journalism_use_case: One-click preservation of a page or social post exactly as rendered in your browser, including content behind a login you legitimately hold — the fastest capture available, and the one reporters will actually use because it takes one keystroke.
pros: Lowest-friction capture in this catalogue: one click, one portable file that opens in any browser forever with no replay software
Captures the rendered state including authenticated pages, so it reaches content crawlers cannot
Extremely active (release v1.38.0 on 2026-11-17, same-day push) with a very large community (22,931 stars)
A CLI exists, so the same engine can be scripted for bulk preservation of a URL list
cons: Not WARC: a single HTML snapshot lacks HTTP headers, request/response records and capture provenance, so it is materially weaker evidence than a WACZ and can be edited afterwards undetectably
Inlining assets alters the document, so the file is a faithful rendering rather than a faithful record of what was transmitted
AGPL-3.0 matters if you redistribute a modified version or embed the engine in a product
99 open issues reflecting the variety of pages users try to capture; very complex pages can produce large files
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 22,931 stars with 99 open issues, release v1.38.0 published 2026-11-17 with same-day push — one of the most actively maintained tools in this catalogue. Its evidentiary limitation relative to WARC is a general property of single-file snapshots, widely discussed in archiving practice.
assessment: Deploy it to every reporter as the default 'save this now' action, and be explicit that it is a reading copy rather than evidence of record. The combination I would standardise for your profile: SingleFile for immediate, universal capture; ArchiveWeb.page or Scoop for the pages that will carry a story. The honest trade-off is that the weaker tool is the one people will actually use, so having both and knowing which is which matters more than mandating the stronger one.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v1.38.0 published the same day, 22,931 stars, 99 open issues. Same-day release and push with a very large user base — exceptional maintenance for a single-maintainer project.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publisher.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: redistributing a modified version or offering it as a network service obliges source publication. Ordinary use as an extension is unaffected.
costs: Free. No infrastructure. Disk for saved files.
privacy: The saved file is written locally with no upload by default — a clean privacy position. As with any authenticated capture, a saved logged-in page may contain personal account context, so treat files accordingly.
alternatives: ArchiveWeb.page for WARC/WACZ capture of the same authenticated content
monolith for a CLI-driven equivalent in bulk
Scoop where provenance metadata is required
summary: Browser extension (and CLI) that saves a complete web page as a single self-contained HTML file with all assets inlined…

name: monolith
purpose: Rust CLI that downloads a web page and embeds all assets (CSS, images, fonts, scripts) into a single portable HTML file.
journalism_use_case: Scriptable bulk preservation of many URLs as portable single-file snapshots for later reading or diffing — the automation counterpart to SingleFile, suitable for preserving a list of a few thousand pages overnight.
pros: 0BSD licence — effectively public domain, the most permissive in this catalogue, with no attribution or copyleft obligation at all
Single static Rust binary with no runtime dependencies, so it deploys anywhere including minimal containers and air-gapped machines
Scriptable for bulk work, which SingleFile's extension form is not
Actively maintained (v2.12.0, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-13) with a large community (15,609 stars)
cons: No JavaScript execution path, so pages whose content is rendered client-side come out empty or partial — a severe limitation for modern portals and social media
Not WARC: same evidentiary weakness as SingleFile, with no headers or capture provenance
Embedded-asset output alters the document and can produce very large files for media-heavy pages
49 open issues; asset-inlining edge cases on complex sites are the recurring theme
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 15,609 stars with 49 open issues, release v2.12.0 (2026-11-02), pushed 2026-11-13, 0BSD licence. The absence of JavaScript execution is documented by the project and is the main functional boundary.
assessment: The right tool for bulk preservation of static pages — statutes, press-release archives, document indexes — where you want portable files and no infrastructure. For anything JavaScript-rendered it will fail quietly, which is the trap: check a sample before running a large job. For your profile the 0BSD licence is worth noting because it makes monolith trivially embeddable in any internal tooling with zero legal consideration, which is rare.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release v2.12.0 (2026-11-02), 15,609 stars, 49 open issues. Regular releases with current commits and a large community.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Captured content belongs to the original publisher.
licence_restrictions: None at all — 0BSD imposes no conditions, not even attribution.
costs: No fee. A single binary; negligible resources. Disk for output files.
privacy: Fetches target assets from your host and writes a local file; nothing is uploaded. The target sees your requests.
alternatives: SingleFile for interactive and authenticated capture
browsertrix-crawler where JavaScript rendering and WARC are needed
wget --warc for bulk static capture with proper WARC output
blockers: No JavaScript execution — fails silently on client-rendered pages
summary: Rust CLI that downloads a web page and embeds all assets (CSS, images, fonts, scripts) into a single portable HTML file

name: WebScrapBook
purpose: Browser extension that captures web pages into an organised personal archive with folder structure, annotations, highlighting and full-text search, optionally backed by a self-hosted server.
journalism_use_case: Build an annotated personal archive of captured pages, with highlighting and notes kept alongside the evidence — useful for a reporter working a long beat who wants their reading, marked up, in one searchable place rather than scattered across bookmarks and screenshots.
pros: Annotation alongside capture is the distinguishing feature: your reasoning about why a page matters is stored with the page, which is exactly what is lost in a bare archive
Optional self-hosted backend means a reporter's archive can be centralised and backed up without a third-party service
Full-text search over captures makes an accumulated personal archive genuinely useful rather than a write-only pile
MPL-2.0 with current activity (pushed 2026-09-28, tag 2.27.3) and a reasonable community (1,251 stars)
cons: Single-user tool by design: no team sharing or collaborative annotation, so it does not scale to an investigation team
Idiosyncratic data format and a modest ecosystem, which creates a migration risk — an archive you cannot easily export into something else is a long-term liability
No release objects on GitHub (tag 2.27.3 only), so pinning and upgrade planning are awkward
Not WARC, so the same evidentiary limitations as other single-file approaches apply
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 1,251 stars with 37 open issues, no release objects, latest tag 2.27.3, last push 2026-09-28, MPL-2.0. Lineage from the long-standing ScrapBook family of Firefox extensions.
assessment: A reasonable personal-productivity choice for an individual investigator, but I would not standardise a newsroom on it because of the format lock-in and single-user design. For your profile the more durable pattern is ArchiveBox for capture plus a notes system you already trust, which separates the archive from the annotation layer and keeps both exportable. If a reporter already uses WebScrapBook happily, the self-hosted backend is worth enabling so their archive is backed up.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-28, no release objects, latest tag 2.27.3, 1,251 stars, 37 open issues. Two months since last push with ongoing tag-based versioning; a mature single-maintainer extension at steady low velocity.
licence_restrictions: MPL-2.0 file-level copyleft on modifications; immaterial for ordinary use.
costs: Free. Optional self-hosted backend is a small service. Negligible.
privacy: Captures go to local disk or your own backend server — no third-party service involved, which is a strong position. The archive accumulates a record of a reporter's research interests, so device and backup security matter.
alternatives: ArchiveBox plus a separate notes system for an exportable, team-visible equivalent
SingleFile for capture without the archive-management layer
Zotero for citation-oriented personal archiving with better export options
summary: Browser extension that captures web pages into an organised personal archive with folder structure, annotations…

name: warcio
purpose: Streaming Python library and CLI for reading, writing, validating and recompressing WARC and ARC files, with record-level access and index generation.
journalism_use_case: Programmatically verify, index and extract records from WARC evidence, or convert captures for analysis pipelines — for example checking that a 40GB capture actually contains the pages you think it does, and extracting their text for search.
pros: Validation is the underrated function: `warcio check` tells you whether a capture is well-formed before you rely on it, which prevents discovering a corrupt archive at the worst moment
Streaming design handles very large WARCs without loading them into memory
Apache-2.0, actively released (v1.8.2, 2026-10-28, same-day push), and the reference Python WARC library in the ecosystem
Simple enough to build bespoke evidence-processing scripts around in an afternoon
cons: Low-level library: no capture or replay capability of its own, so it is only useful inside a larger workflow
63 open issues against 486 stars — a modest backlog for a utility library but indicative of edge cases in malformed WARCs
Working with it requires understanding the WARC record model, which is a small but real learning curve
Does nothing to help a non-engineer
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 486 stars with 63 open issues, release v1.8.2 on 2026-10-28 with same-day push, Apache-2.0. Its position as the standard Python WARC library is evidenced by dependency use across the archiving ecosystem.
assessment: Adopt it as soon as you hold WARCs — the validation and extraction functions are what make an archive auditable rather than opaque. For your profile the specific practice worth adopting is to run a validation and record-count check on every capture as part of the workflow, and store the result alongside the archive. That turns 'we captured the site' into 'we captured 4,312 records, verified well-formed on this date', which is a materially stronger evidentiary statement.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-28, latest release v1.8.2 published the same day, 486 stars, 63 open issues. Current releases under Webrecorder maintenance as part of a coherent suite.
costs: No fee. Pure Python, negligible resources.
privacy: Operates on local files only with no network calls — safe on an air-gapped evidence machine.
alternatives: py-wacz for packaging rather than record-level manipulation
OutbackCDX for indexing a large collection for lookup
pywb, which bundles much of this functionality for replay purposes
summary: Streaming Python library and CLI for reading, writing, validating and recompressing WARC and ARC files…

name: warcprox
purpose: HTTP/HTTPS man-in-the-middle proxy that writes every request and response passing through it into WARC files, used as the recording layer for browser-driven crawls.
journalism_use_case: Record every request made during a browsing or scraping session into WARC, so collection and evidence capture happen in one pass — you browse or scrape normally and come away with an evidentiary record of everything the server actually sent.
pros: Capture-by-proxy means any tool or browser you point at it produces WARC output, including tools that have no archiving support of their own — a genuinely elegant architecture
Records the actual HTTP exchanges including headers, which is what gives WARC its evidentiary value over rendered snapshots
Apache-adjacent open licensing, actively released (v2.13.1, 2026-05-11) under Internet Archive maintenance, and the recording layer beneath brozzler
Pairs with any scraping workflow, so an existing Scrapy or Playwright collection can become evidentiary with no code changes
cons: All proxied traffic, including credentials and session tokens, is written into your WARCs — a serious handling consideration that is easy to overlook and makes the output highly sensitive
Requires installing a local CA certificate in the browser to intercept TLS, which is a security-posture change on the capture machine that must be reversed afterwards
The licence is declared only in packaging metadata rather than a LICENSE file (GitHub reports no SPDX), so the GPL-2.0-or-later position needs confirmation for compliance records
Operator-level tool with 27 open issues and six months since the last push (2026-06-17); not something a reporter would run
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 469 stars with 27 open issues, release v2.13.1 (2026-05-11), last push 2026-06-17, SPDX none with GPL-2.0-or-later declared in packaging metadata (verified session 1, retained). Production use at the Internet Archive via brozzler.
assessment: Powerful and genuinely useful for turning any collection into evidence, with two cautions I would treat as mandatory for your context. First, WARCs produced by proxying a logged-in session contain your credentials and tokens — encrypt them and restrict access, or scrub before sharing. Second, the local CA certificate weakens the capture machine's TLS trust model while installed, so use a dedicated capture VM rather than a reporter's daily laptop.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-06-17, latest release v2.13.1 (2026-05-11), SPDX none, 469 stars, 27 open issues. Five months since last push on a mature component under institutional maintenance; stable rather than declining, since brozzler's continued releases depend on it.
licence: GPL-2.0-or-later (declared in packaging metadata; no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no SPDX)
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0-or-later per packaging metadata. The absence of a LICENSE file is a compliance-record weakness — cite the packaging metadata explicitly if your legal team requires it.
costs: No fee. A small Python service plus WARC storage. Negligible infrastructure; non-trivial setup time for the CA certificate arrangement.
privacy: All proxied traffic, including credentials and session tokens, is written into your WARCs — treat output as highly sensitive. The local CA certificate installation changes the trust posture of the capture machine for as long as it is present.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler, which handles capture internally without a proxy or CA certificate
mitmproxy for traffic inspection without WARC output
Scoop or ArchiveWeb.page for capture without changing the machine's trust store
blockers: WARCs contain credentials and session tokens from proxied traffic; requires installing a local CA certificate
summary: HTTP/HTTPS man-in-the-middle proxy that writes every request and response passing through it into WARC files…

name: py-wacz
purpose: Python library and CLI that packages WARC files into the WACZ (Web Archive Collection Zipped) format, generating the required indexes, pages list and optional datapackage metadata.
journalism_use_case: Package captures into a single self-contained WACZ for archiving, sharing with lawyers, or embedding in a published story — the step that converts loose WARC files into something a colleague can open in ReplayWeb.page with no instructions.
pros: Produces the one archive format that a non-technical recipient can actually open (via ReplayWeb.page), which is the practical difference between holding evidence and being able to show it
Includes index and page-list generation, so the resulting WACZ is browsable rather than just a zip of WARCs
MIT licensed with current releases (v0.6.0, 2026-09-10) under Webrecorder maintenance
Small and scriptable, so it drops into a capture pipeline as a final packaging step
cons: Niche utility with a small user base (63 stars) and a relatively high open-issue count for its size (21), reflecting spec-tracking churn
Spec-tracking rather than feature-rich: it follows the WACZ specification, so its capabilities are bounded by that spec's evolution
Does nothing on its own — requires WARC inputs from a separate capture tool
If you use browsertrix-crawler, WACZ output is already produced, making this redundant for the common path
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 63 stars with 21 open issues, release v0.6.0 (2026-09-10), last push 2026-10-13, MIT. The WACZ specification itself is a Webrecorder-led effort, so this is the reference implementation.
assessment: Needed only if you produce WARCs by some route other than browsertrix-crawler — for example warcprox-proxied scraping, Heritrix crawls, or wget --warc captures — and want them in a shareable form. That is a real case: a Heritrix collection packaged as WACZ becomes something counsel can review. Otherwise it is already covered by your capture tool, and I would not seek it out.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-13, latest release v0.6.0 (2026-09-10), 63 stars, 21 open issues. Current releases as the reference implementation of a specification the maintainer leads.
costs: No fee. Local file packaging; negligible resources.
privacy: Local file packaging only, no network calls. Note that packaging does not sanitise content — credentials captured in a WARC remain in the WACZ.
alternatives: browsertrix-crawler, which emits WACZ directly
warcio for record-level WARC work without packaging
Distributing raw WARCs plus pywb if the recipient has infrastructure
summary: Python library and CLI that packages WARC files into the WACZ (Web Archive Collection Zipped) format…

name: OutbackCDX
purpose: RocksDB-backed CDX index server that provides fast URL and timestamp lookup over large WARC collections, compatible with pywb and OpenWayback front ends.
journalism_use_case: Index a large in-house WARC collection so investigators can query by URL and timestamp like the public Wayback Machine — the component that makes a multi-terabyte capture collection usable rather than theoretically searchable.
pros: Solves the scaling problem that makes large private archives unusable: without a proper CDX index, URL lookup over terabytes of WARC is impractically slow
Compatible with pywb and OpenWayback, so it slots into the standard replay stack without custom work
Apache-2.0 under IIPC stewardship — the web-archiving standards body — which is a strong continuity signal for long-lived infrastructure
Actively maintained (1.3.0, 2026-09-30; pushed 2026-11-13) with a small clean backlog
cons: Infrastructure component only: it requires a pywb or OpenWayback front end and real operations capacity, so it is the third piece of a three-piece stack
Java plus RocksDB storage is another operational idiom to maintain alongside your other systems
Tiny community (46 stars, 19 open issues), so operational knowledge comes from IIPC community documentation rather than Stack Overflow
Only worth deploying above a scale most newsrooms never reach — below a few hundred GB, pywb alone is fine
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 46 stars with 19 open issues, release 1.3.0 (2026-09-30), last push 2026-11-13, Apache-2.0. Used by national and institutional web archives within the IIPC community, which is the relevant production context.
assessment: Only relevant if your capture programme grows to the point where pywb's own indexing becomes the bottleneck — which happens around the multi-terabyte mark, not before. For your profile I would note it as the known upgrade path rather than deploy it now: build with pywb, and if the collection grows large enough that lookups become slow, OutbackCDX is the standard answer and it slots in without changing the rest of the stack.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-13, latest release 1.3.0 (2026-09-30), 46 stars, 19 open issues. Current releases under IIPC stewardship with institutional production use; small community reflects the narrow operator audience rather than low maintenance.
costs: No fee. Infrastructure estimate: a JVM service plus RocksDB storage for the index (a fraction of the WARC collection size) — modest relative to the WARC storage it serves. Assumptions: self-hosted alongside an existing archive.
privacy: Index queries stay within your infrastructure — no external calls. As with pywb, the index must not be publicly exposed, since it reveals every URL you have captured.
alternatives: pywb's built-in indexing for collections below the terabyte scale
CDXJ files generated by warcio for simple lookup needs
OpenWayback for an alternative front end
summary: RocksDB-backed CDX index server that provides fast URL and timestamp lookup over large WARC collections…

name: yt-dlp
purpose: Command-line media downloader supporting well over a thousand sites, retrieving video, audio, subtitles, thumbnails and uploader metadata at the highest available quality, with extensive format and post-processing control.
journalism_use_case: The workhorse for securing a copy of social video before deletion — pulling the highest available bitrate (crucial because compression destroys the artefacts forensic analysis relies on), plus uploader metadata, upload timestamps, subtitles and thumbnails. For verification work, the bitrate point is decisive: a re-encoded copy from a screen recording is forensically useless.
pros: Highest-available-quality retrieval preserves the forensic signal that any re-encoding destroys, which makes it the correct first step before any media verification
Captures uploader metadata, upload timestamps, subtitles and thumbnails alongside the media — often the evidentiary context that matters more than the video itself
Unlicense (public domain) and extraordinarily active (208,589 stars, release 2026.10.26, pushed 2026-11-17), with extractors updated continuously as platforms change
Covers over a thousand sites, so it works on the regional and niche platforms where much relevant material actually lives
cons: A capture tool with no verification logic and no authenticity judgement — it tells you nothing about whether the content is real
Extractors break frequently when platforms change, so you must pin or update often and expect occasional silent format downgrades that quietly reduce quality

Contacts the target platform directly from the operator's machine, so your IP and request pattern are visible to that platform — and for a high-volume capture campaign that is an identifiable footprint
Downloading may breach platform terms of service and, depending on jurisdiction and purpose, raises copyright questions that are a legal rather than technical matter
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 208,589 stars with 2,790 open issues, release 2026.10.26, pushed 2026-11-17 — the largest community in this catalogue, with a backlog that reflects the constant churn of platform extractors rather than neglect. The project itself notes platform-specific constraints in its documentation.
assessment: Adopt unconditionally as the media-capture step — the quality-preservation property alone makes it non-negotiable before verification work. For your profile the operational points are: capture from a dedicated egress rather than the newsroom address when the uploader should not know you are looking, record the yt-dlp version and the full metadata JSON alongside the media so the capture is documented, and update frequently because a stale extractor silently gives you a lower-quality file. Treat the terms-of-service and copyright questions as editorial decisions, taken knowingly.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release 2026.10.26, 208,589 stars, 2,790 open issues. Continuous releases on a date-based scheme with same-day commits; the huge issue count is intrinsic to maintaining a thousand platform extractors against constant upstream change.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Downloaded content belongs to the original rights holders.
licence_restrictions: None from the licence — the Unlicense is a public-domain dedication. The real constraints are external: platform terms of service and copyright in the downloaded material, both of which are editorial and legal judgements rather than licence issues.
costs: No fee. FFmpeg/FFprobe strongly recommended; yt-dlp-ejs with a JavaScript runtime for some sites. Storage for high-bitrate media is the real cost and grows quickly. Estimate.
privacy: Contacts the target platform directly from the operator's machine, so IP and request pattern are visible to that platform. For sensitive subjects, capture from a dedicated egress. Downloaded metadata may include personal information about uploaders, which attracts your own data-protection obligations.
alternatives: gallery-dl for image-focused platform capture
browsertrix-crawler or ArchiveWeb.page to capture the surrounding page as evidence of context
Platform-specific archival tools where yt-dlp lacks an extractor
summary: Command-line media downloader supporting well over a thousand sites, retrieving video, audio, subtitles…
